nerve: Bundles of nerve fibres (axons) in connective tissue that carry signals between the central nervous system and the body: sensory fibres in, motor fibres out.
fiber: Long thread-like structures. In muscle, a fibre is one whole multinucleated muscle cell; in connective tissue, fibres are collagen, elastic or reticular protein strands in the matrix.
protein: Large molecules built from chains of amino acids joined by peptide bonds. They do most of the cell's work: enzymes, structure, transport, signalling and contraction.
artery: Vessels that carry blood away from the heart, with thick muscular, elastic walls to withstand high pressure.
tendon: A cord of dense regular connective tissue (parallel collagen fibres) that attaches muscle to bone and transmits its pull.
skeletal-muscle: Striated, voluntary muscle made of long multinucleated fibres attached to bones; it moves the body, holds posture and produces heat.
epithelium: Tissue of tightly packed cells with little matrix that covers surfaces and lines cavities and ducts, resting on a basement membrane. It is avascular.
joint: A site where two or more bones meet. Classified as fibrous, cartilaginous or synovial, which decides how much they move.
epidermis: The outer layer of the skin: keratinized stratified squamous epithelium, avascular and nourished by diffusion from the dermis.
dermis: The connective-tissue layer of the skin under the epidermis: a thin loose papillary layer over a thick dense irregular reticular layer, carrying vessels, nerves and glands.
myosin: The motor protein of the thick filament. Its heads bind actin and, powered by ATP, pull the thin filaments toward the centre of the sarcomere.
receptor: A protein that binds a specific signal (a hormone, neurotransmitter or other ligand) and triggers a response; in sensation, a structure that detects a stimulus.
actin: The protein of the thin filament. Myosin heads bind its active sites and pull it during contraction; tropomyosin and troponin control access to those sites.
nucleus: The membrane-bound organelle holding the cell's DNA. Its number and position (central, peripheral) help tell muscle types apart.
ligament: A band of dense regular connective tissue that joins bone to bone, stabilizing a joint and limiting its movement.
smooth-muscle: Non-striated, involuntary muscle of spindle-shaped cells with one central nucleus, found in the walls of vessels and hollow organs.
branche: Smaller vessels or nerves that split off from a larger trunk to supply a region.
reflex: A rapid, predictable, involuntary response to a stimulus, carried by a reflex arc without needing conscious control.
cardiac-muscle: Striated, involuntary muscle of the heart: short branched cells with one or two central nuclei, joined end to end by intercalated discs.
neuron: A nerve cell: a cell body with dendrites that receive signals and a single axon that carries action potentials to other cells.
sarcomere: The smallest functional unit of striated muscle: the segment of a myofibril between two Z discs. It shortens as thin filaments slide over thick ones.
blood-vessel: The tubes that carry blood: arteries away from the heart, capillaries for exchange, veins back to the heart.
columnar: Epithelial cells taller than they are wide, with nuclei near the base. They line the gut (absorption and secretion) and, pseudostratified and ciliated, the airways.
capsule: A connective-tissue envelope around a structure, such as a joint capsule, an organ capsule or the capsule of an encapsulated nerve ending.
cartilage: Firm, flexible, avascular connective tissue of chondrocytes in lacunae within a gel-like matrix. Types: hyaline, elastic and fibrocartilage.
spinal: Relating to the spinal cord or the vertebral column, as in spinal nerves, spinal reflexes and spinal segments.
myofibril: Long bundles of thin and thick myofilaments inside a muscle fibre, arranged end to end in sarcomeres; they give the fibre its striations.
origin: The attachment of a muscle that stays fixed when it contracts, usually the proximal one.
cuboidal: Epithelial cells about as tall as they are wide, with round central nuclei; they line kidney tubules and small gland ducts.
sarcolemma: The plasma membrane of a muscle fibre. It conducts the muscle action potential and folds inward to form the T-tubules.
glucogenic: Describes amino acids whose carbon skeletons can be turned into glucose (through pyruvate or citric-acid-cycle intermediates).
ketogenic: Describes amino acids broken down to acetyl-CoA or acetoacetate, which can form ketone bodies and fat but not glucose; leucine and lysine are purely ketogenic.
lymph-node: Small bean-shaped organs along lymphatic vessels that filter lymph; B-cell follicles in the cortex, T cells in the paracortex, plasma cells in the medulla.
relaxation: The return of a muscle to rest after contraction: Ca²⁺ is pumped back into the SR, tropomyosin covers actin again and crossbridges stop forming.
vertebrae: The bones of the spinal column (7 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, plus sacrum and coccyx), each with a body, an arch and processes around the vertebral foramen.
melanocyte: A pigment cell in the basal layer of the epidermis that makes melanin and passes it to nearby keratinocytes through its long processes.
twitch: A single brief contraction of a muscle in response to one stimulus: latent period, contraction, then relaxation.
fatigue: A fall in a muscle's force despite continued stimulation, from depleted energy stores, accumulated metabolites, or failure at the nerve or neuromuscular junction.
heart: The muscular pump in the middle mediastinum whose four chambers drive blood through the pulmonary and systemic circulations; its wall is cardiac muscle.
secretion: Release of a product from a cell or gland. Exocrine glands secrete by merocrine (exocytosis), apocrine or holocrine (whole cell) mechanisms.
thyroid: A butterfly-shaped endocrine gland in front of the trachea that makes thyroid hormones (and calcitonin); the recurrent laryngeal nerve runs close behind it.
cross-section: A cut across a structure at right angles to its long axis. Muscle fibres cut this way appear as round or polygonal profiles.
macrophage: Large phagocytic cells derived from monocytes that engulf microbes and debris and present antigens; called Kupffer cells in the liver.
mesoderm: The middle germ layer of the embryo. It forms muscle, bone, cartilage, the dermis, the heart, blood and vessels, the kidneys and the gonads.
sebaceous-gland: A holocrine gland that opens into a hair follicle and secretes oily sebum to lubricate the hair and skin; absent from the palms and soles.
tricep: Triceps brachii, the three-headed muscle at the back of the arm that extends the elbow; supplied by the radial nerve. Its tendon reflex tests C7.
bicep: Biceps brachii, the two-headed muscle at the front of the arm that flexes the elbow and supinates the forearm; supplied by the musculocutaneous nerve. Its reflex tests C5–C6.
cranium: The skull: the neurocranium enclosing the brain and the viscerocranium forming the face.
extension: A movement that straightens a joint or increases the angle between parts; the opposite of flexion.
pressure: Force per area. In the body it appears as blood (hydrostatic) pressure, oncotic pressure from plasma proteins, and the deep touch sensed by skin receptors.
striated: Showing regular light and dark cross-bands under the microscope, from the ordered sarcomeres of skeletal and cardiac muscle.
endomysium: A very thin layer of fine reticular fibres around each muscle fibre, carrying capillaries right up to the cell.
fascicle: A bundle of muscle fibres (or nerve fibres) wrapped in its own connective-tissue sheath, the perimysium (or perineurium).
foramina: Openings through bone that let nerves and vessels pass, such as those of the skull base.
i-band: The light (isotropic) band of a sarcomere containing only thin actin filaments; it is bisected by the Z line and shortens during contraction.
internal-jugular-vein: The main vein draining the brain, face and neck. It leaves the skull through the jugular foramen and runs in the carotid sheath to join the subclavian vein.
muscle-tissue: Tissue of elongated cells packed with contractile actin and myosin filaments. Its three types are skeletal, cardiac and smooth.
plane: Imaginary flat surfaces used to describe sections and positions: the median, sagittal, frontal (coronal) and transverse planes.
skeleton-trunci: The skeleton of the trunk: the vertebral column, the ribs and the sternum.
troponin: The regulatory protein complex on the thin filament (TnC binds Ca²⁺, TnI inhibits, TnT binds tropomyosin) that switches contraction on when calcium rises.
crossbridge: The attachment of a myosin head to actin. Cycles of crossbridge binding, pulling and releasing slide the filaments and make force.
desmosome: A spot-like cell junction that rivets neighbouring cells together by anchoring intermediate (keratin) filaments, giving mechanical strength.
intercalated-disc: The step-like junctions joining cardiac muscle cells end to end, with desmosomes and fasciae adherentes for strength and gap junctions for electrical coupling.
involuntary: Not under conscious control: cardiac and smooth muscle, supplied by the autonomic nervous system.
latent-period: The short delay between a stimulus (the action potential) and the start of contraction, while calcium is released and crossbridges begin to form.
lymphocyte: White blood cells of adaptive immunity, with a large round nucleus and a thin rim of cytoplasm: B cells make antibodies, T cells attack infected cells and coordinate.
muscle-fiber: One skeletal muscle cell: long, cylindrical and multinucleated, filled with myofibrils.
sciatic-nerve: The largest nerve of the body (L4–S3). It leaves the pelvis below the piriformis and runs down the back of the thigh, splitting into the tibial and common fibular nerves.
shorten: What a muscle does in contraction: its sarcomeres get shorter as the thin filaments slide over the thick ones, though the filaments themselves keep their length.
thick-skin: Skin of the palms and soles with a very thick stratum corneum and a stratum lucidum, many sweat glands, and no hair or sebaceous glands.
titin: A huge elastic protein running from the Z disc to the M line that holds thick filaments centred and makes the passive tension of a stretched muscle.
albumin: The most abundant plasma protein (about 35–50 g/L), made in the liver. It makes most of the plasma oncotic pressure and carries fatty acids, hormones and drugs.
basement-membrane: A thin sheet of extracellular matrix (basal lamina plus reticular lamina) under every epithelium, anchoring it to the connective tissue below.
gastrocnemius: The two-headed superficial calf muscle that plantar-flexes the ankle and flexes the knee; it joins the soleus in the Achilles tendon. The frog gastrocnemius is used in the wet lab.
intercostal: The muscles between the ribs (external, internal, innermost) that move the ribs in breathing, with their intercostal nerves and vessels.
loose-connective-tissue: Areolar tissue: loosely arranged fibres, many cells and plenty of ground substance, which fills spaces, supports epithelia and carries small vessels.
m-line: The dark line in the middle of the A band, where proteins such as myomesin link the thick filaments together.
median-nerve: A nerve of the brachial plexus (C5–T1) that runs through the cubital fossa and the carpal tunnel to the forearm flexors and thenar muscles; injury gives the hand of benediction.
motor-unit: One motor neuron plus all the skeletal muscle fibres it innervates; they always contract together.
radial-nerve: The brachial plexus nerve (C5–T1) that winds round the humerus in the radial groove to supply the arm and forearm extensors; injury gives wrist drop.
sternum: The flat breastbone in the front of the chest, made of the manubrium, body and xiphoid process; the costal cartilages of the upper ribs join it.
striation: The regular alternating light (I) and dark (A) bands across skeletal and cardiac muscle fibres, from aligned sarcomeres.
summation: The addition of force when a second stimulus arrives before the muscle has relaxed from the first, so the twitches build on each other.
synapse: The junction where a neuron passes a signal to another cell, usually by releasing a neurotransmitter across a narrow cleft.
tropomyosin: A long protein lying along the thin filament that covers actin's myosin-binding sites at rest; troponin moves it aside when calcium rises.
avascular: Without blood vessels; such tissues (epithelium, cartilage) are nourished by diffusion from nearby connective tissue.
carotid: Relating to the carotid arteries of the neck: the common carotid divides into the internal (brain) and external (face and neck) carotids at about C4.
clavicle: The S-shaped collarbone joining the sternum to the scapula; it holds the upper limb away from the trunk and is the most commonly fractured bone.
fatty-acid: Long hydrocarbon chains with a carboxyl group, the building blocks of fats and phospholipids and a major fuel oxidized for ATP.
processe: Projections from a bone (such as the spinous and transverse processes of a vertebra) or from a cell, such as the long processes of a melanocyte or neuron.
stratified: Epithelium with two or more layers of cells, named after the shape of the top layer; it resists abrasion.
stratum-basale: The deepest layer of the epidermis: one row of cuboidal to columnar stem cells on the basement membrane, dividing to renew the skin, with melanocytes and Merkel cells.
translation: Protein synthesis on ribosomes, where the codons of mRNA are read and tRNAs bring the matching amino acids to build the chain.
transverse-section: A section cut across the long axis (a cross-section); skeletal muscle fibres in it show peripheral nuclei and Cohnheim's areas.
voluntary: Under conscious control: skeletal muscle, supplied by somatic motor neurons.
apical: Toward the apex or free top: the apical surface of an epithelial cell faces the lumen; the apical lymph nodes sit at the top of the axilla.
chromosome: A long strand of DNA packed with proteins that carries genes; human body cells have 46 (23 pairs).
codon: A sequence of three mRNA bases that codes for one amino acid or a stop signal during translation.
ectoderm: The outer germ layer of the embryo. It forms the epidermis and its appendages, the nervous system and the neural crest.
epithelial-cell: The cells that make up epithelium: closely joined by junctions, polarized into apical, lateral and basal surfaces, and resting on a basement membrane.
neuromuscular-junction: The synapse between a motor neuron and a skeletal muscle fibre, where released acetylcholine binds nicotinic receptors on the motor end plate to start the muscle action potential.
nucleotide: The building block of DNA and RNA: a nitrogenous base, a five-carbon sugar and a phosphate group.
brachial-plexus: The network of nerves from the ventral rami of C5–T1 that supplies the upper limb, giving off the musculocutaneous, axillary, radial, median and ulnar nerves.
dermal-papillae: Finger-like projections of the papillary dermis into the epidermis, carrying capillaries and Meissner's corpuscles; they anchor the two layers and form fingerprints.
epimysium: The outermost layer of dense irregular connective tissue, surrounding the entire muscle.
hypodermis: The subcutaneous layer under the dermis: loose connective tissue and fat that insulates, stores energy and anchors the skin; it holds Pacinian corpuscles.
multinucleated: Having many nuclei in one cell, as in skeletal muscle fibres, formed by the fusion of myoblasts.
perimysium: A layer of dense irregular connective tissue around each fascicle (bundle of fibres). Larger vessels and nerves travel here.
spinosum: Short for stratum spinosum, the layer of the epidermis whose cells look spiny because of their many desmosomes.
stratum-spinosum: The epidermal layer above the basale: several rows of polygonal keratinocytes joined by desmosomes (the 'spines'), with Langerhans cells.
thin-skin: Skin covering most of the body: a thin stratum corneum, no stratum lucidum, with hair follicles and sebaceous glands.
tibia: The medial, weight-bearing bone of the leg, joining the femur at the knee and the talus at the ankle.
transcription: The copying of a DNA gene into RNA by RNA polymerase, the first step of gene expression.
ulnar-nerve: A brachial plexus nerve (C8–T1) that passes behind the medial epicondyle (the 'funny bone') to supply most intrinsic hand muscles; injury gives claw hand.
z-disc: The line at each end of a sarcomere that anchors the thin filaments (with α-actinin); Z discs move closer together as the muscle contracts.
autonomic: Relating to the autonomic nervous system, which controls involuntary functions such as heart rate, glands and smooth muscle.
keratinocyte: The main cell of the epidermis. Keratinocytes are made in the stratum basale and fill with keratin as they move up, dying to form the protective stratum corneum.
langerhan-cell: A dendritic immune cell of the epidermis, mostly in the stratum spinosum, that captures antigens and carries them to lymph nodes.
longitudinal-section: A section cut along the long axis of a structure; skeletal muscle cut this way shows its cross-striations and peripheral nuclei.
merkel-cell: A touch-sensitive cell in the basal epidermis, most numerous in thick skin, that forms a Merkel disc with a sensory nerve ending for light touch.
motor-end-plate: The specialized folded region of the sarcolemma under the motor nerve ending, rich in acetylcholine receptors.
radius: The lateral forearm bone, on the thumb side; it rotates around the ulna in pronation and supination.
rib-i: The first rib: the shortest, broadest, flattest and most sharply curved, grooved by the subclavian artery and vein.
acetylcholine: The neurotransmitter released at the neuromuscular junction (and in parts of the autonomic system); it opens ion channels on the muscle to start contraction.
anucleate: Without a nucleus, like mature red blood cells, platelets and the dead cells of the stratum corneum.
arrector-pili: A small band of smooth muscle from the dermis to a hair follicle; its contraction raises the hair (goosebumps).
efferent: Carrying signals away from the central nervous system toward muscles and glands (motor); the opposite of afferent.
erythrocyte: Red blood cells: anucleate biconcave discs (about 7.5 µm) packed with haemoglobin to carry oxygen.
femoral-nerve: The largest branch of the lumbar plexus (L2–L4). It passes under the inguinal ligament into the femoral triangle to supply the quadriceps; it carries the knee-jerk reflex.
flexion: A movement that bends a joint or decreases the angle between parts; the opposite of extension.
gap-junction: Channels of connexons (six connexins each) linking the cytoplasm of neighbouring cells, so ions and small molecules pass directly; they couple cardiac cells electrically.
h-zone: The lighter centre of the A band, where only thick myosin filaments are present; it narrows as the muscle contracts.
keratinized-stratified-squamous-epitheli: Stratified squamous epithelium whose surface cells are dead, flattened and full of keratin, forming the waterproof, abrasion-resistant epidermis.
medial-epicondyle: The bony prominence on the inner side of the lower humerus; the ulnar nerve passes behind it and the forearm flexors arise from it.
medulla: The inner part of an organ or structure, such as the core of a hair, the lymph node medulla or the medulla oblongata of the brainstem.
meissner-s-corpuscle: Encapsulated touch receptors in the dermal papillae, most numerous in the fingertips and lips, that sense light, fine touch.
notochord: A rod of mesoderm along the embryo's midline that induces the neural tube and vertebrae; its remnant is the nucleus pulposus of the intervertebral discs.
respiratory-tract: The airways from the nose to the alveoli, mostly lined by ciliated pseudostratified columnar epithelium with goblet cells.
sarcoplasmic-reticulum: The muscle fibre's specialized smooth ER, wrapped round each myofibril, which stores calcium and releases it when the fibre is stimulated.
squamous: Flat, scale-like epithelial cells. Simple squamous lines vessels and body cavities; stratified squamous forms the epidermis and lines the mouth and oesophagus.
stratum-corneum: The outermost layer of the epidermis: 15–20 or more layers of dead, flattened, anucleate cells full of keratin, constantly shed (desquamation).
striated-muscle: Muscle with cross-striations from ordered sarcomeres: skeletal and cardiac muscle.
treppe: The 'staircase' effect: successive twitches, each after complete relaxation, grow slightly stronger at first as calcium and temperature rise in the fibre.
triangular: Three-sided in shape, as in the posterior fontanelle, the triangular bone (triquetrum) or the triangles of the neck.
carpal: The eight small wrist bones in two rows: scaphoid, lunate, triquetrum, pisiform; trapezium, trapezoid, capitate, hamate.
genome: The complete set of genetic information (DNA) of an organism; the human genome is about 3 billion base pairs.
hemidesmosome: Half-desmosomes on the basal surface of epithelial cells that anchor them to the basement membrane rather than to another cell.
isometric: Same length: a contraction in which the muscle develops tension without shortening, because the load is too heavy to move.
mast-cell: Connective-tissue cells packed with granules of histamine and heparin; their degranulation drives allergic and inflammatory reactions.
merocrine: Secretion by exocytosis, the cell staying intact, as in eccrine sweat glands and salivary glands.
sheath: Connective-tissue wrappings: in muscle the epimysium (whole muscle), perimysium (fascicle) and endomysium (fibre); also tendon, root and nerve sheaths.
stratum-lucidum: A thin clear layer of flattened, anucleate cells containing eleidin between the granulosum and corneum, found only in thick skin.
tetanus: A sustained contraction from stimuli so frequent the muscle can't relax between them; also the disease caused by Clostridium tetani toxin, which produces spastic paralysis.
tibial-nerve: The larger terminal branch of the sciatic nerve. It runs through the popliteal fossa and behind the medial malleolus to supply the calf and sole; it carries the ankle reflex.
ciliated: Bearing cilia, motile hair-like projections that beat to move mucus or fluid along a surface, as in the airways and uterine tubes.
deep-dermis: The reticular layer of the dermis: dense irregular connective tissue with thick collagen bundles, holding hair follicles, glands and Pacinian corpuscles.
facial-nerve: Cranial nerve VII. It leaves the skull through the stylomastoid foramen and supplies the muscles of facial expression, taste to the front of the tongue, and the lacrimal and salivary glands.
fibroblast: The main cell of connective tissue, which makes collagen, elastic fibres and the ground substance of the matrix.
flattened-cell: Thin, flat cells, such as the squamous surface cells of an epithelium or the lamellae of the capsule round an encapsulated nerve ending.
fontanelle: Membrane-covered gaps between the skull bones of an infant: the anterior closes at about 18–24 months, the posterior at 2–3 months.
fused-tetanus: Complete tetanus: stimuli come so fast that the twitches fuse into one smooth, sustained maximal contraction with no relaxation between them.
holocrine: Secretion in which the whole cell fills with product, dies and breaks down to become the secretion, as in the sebaceous glands making sebum.
insertion: The movable attachment of a muscle, usually the distal one, which is pulled toward the origin when it contracts.
light-touch: Fine, gentle touch sensation, sensed by Meissner's corpuscles and Merkel discs in the superficial skin.
microvilli: Short, finger-like projections of the apical membrane (with an actin core) that greatly increase the absorptive surface, forming a brush border.
mitochondria: Double-membraned organelles that make most of the cell's ATP by aerobic respiration; abundant in muscle fibres.
nucleus-pulposus: The gel-like core of an intervertebral disc, a remnant of the notochord, that absorbs pressure; it can herniate through the anulus fibrosus.
phosphate: A phosphorus–oxygen group (PO₄³⁻) in nucleotides, ATP, phospholipids and bone mineral; transferring it stores and releases energy.
pseudostratified: A simple epithelium that only looks layered because its nuclei sit at different heights; every cell touches the basement membrane. Lines most of the airway.
rotation: Movement of a bone around its own long axis, medially (inward) or laterally (outward).
sarcoplasm: The cytoplasm of a muscle fibre, mostly filled with myofibrils and rich in glycogen and myoglobin.
simple-squamous: One layer of flat cells, thin enough for fast diffusion and filtration; it lines vessels (endothelium), body cavities (mesothelium) and alveoli.
t-tubule: Transverse tubules: inward extensions of the sarcolemma that carry the action potential deep into the fibre next to the sarcoplasmic reticulum.
transitional: Urothelium, the stratified epithelium of the urinary tract whose dome-shaped surface cells flatten as the bladder stretches.
achille-tendon: The calcaneal tendon, the strongest tendon in the body, joining the gastrocnemius and soleus to the calcaneus; tapping it tests the S1 ankle reflex.
apocrine: Glands that release secretion with part of the apical cytoplasm; the apocrine sweat glands of the axilla and groin open into hair follicles.
axillary-nerve: A brachial plexus nerve (C5–C6) that winds round the surgical neck of the humerus to supply the deltoid and teres minor.
bicep-femoris: The lateral hamstring muscle at the back of the thigh, which flexes the knee and extends the hip.
cilia: Motile hair-like projections of the apical surface, with a 9+2 microtubule core, that beat together to move mucus or fluid; found in the airways and uterine tubes.
cohnheim-s-areas: The island-like pattern of myofibril bundles seen inside a skeletal muscle fiber cut in cross-section.
concentric-lamellae: Layers arranged in rings around a centre, like the onion-like capsule of a Pacinian corpuscle or the bone layers of an osteon.
costal-facet: Small articular surfaces on thoracic vertebrae where the heads and tubercles of the ribs join them.
creatine-phosphate: A high-energy store in muscle that quickly regenerates ATP from ADP (via creatine kinase), fuelling about 10–15 seconds of maximal effort.
dense-irregular-connective-tissue: Connective tissue with thick collagen bundles running in many directions, resisting pull from all sides; found in the dermis, organ capsules and the epimysium.
eccrine-sweat-gland: The common sweat glands over the whole body: simple coiled tubular, merocrine, opening directly onto the skin to cool it with watery sweat.
endoderm: The inner germ layer of the embryo. It forms the lining of the gut and airways and the liver, pancreas, thyroid and bladder lining.
excitation-contraction-coupling: The link between the muscle action potential and contraction: the signal runs down the T-tubules and makes the sarcoplasmic reticulum release calcium.
globulin: A group of plasma proteins (α, β and γ). Gamma globulins are the antibodies (immunoglobulins); others carry hormones, metals and lipids.
granulocyte: White blood cells with visible cytoplasmic granules: neutrophils, eosinophils and basophils.
inguinal-ligament: The rolled lower edge of the external oblique aponeurosis, from the anterior superior iliac spine to the pubic tubercle; it roofs the femoral triangle.
interossea: Between bones: the interosseous membranes and the interossei muscles between the metacarpals or metatarsals.
isotonic: Same tension: a contraction in which the muscle changes length while its tension stays about the same, moving a load.
lucidum: Short for stratum lucidum, the clear layer of thick skin between the granulosum and corneum.
mastication: Chewing, done by the temporalis, masseter and medial pterygoid (closing the jaw) and the lateral pterygoid (opening it), all supplied by the mandibular nerve.
maximal-stimulus: The weakest stimulus that recruits every motor unit in a muscle, giving its largest single twitch; stronger stimuli add no more force.
monosynaptic: A reflex with one synapse, directly from sensory neuron to motor neuron, like the stretch (knee-jerk) reflex.
muscle-type: The three types of muscle tissue: skeletal (striated, voluntary), cardiac (striated, involuntary) and smooth (non-striated, involuntary).
olecranon: The hook-like upper end of the ulna that forms the point of the elbow; the triceps inserts on it.
plantar-flexion: Pointing the foot downward at the ankle, done mainly by the gastrocnemius and soleus.
polysynaptic: A reflex with interneurons between the sensory and motor neurons, such as the withdrawal reflex.
posterior-triangle: The region of the neck between the sternocleidomastoid, trapezius and clavicle, holding the accessory nerve, brachial plexus trunks and the subclavian artery.
rib-ii: The second rib, about twice as long as the first, joining the sternum at the sternal angle; it is the landmark for counting ribs.
ruffini: Ruffini endings: encapsulated, spray-like nerve endings in the dermis and joint capsules that sense skin stretch and sustained pressure.
scalp: The soft tissue over the skull in five layers: skin, dense connective tissue, aponeurosis, loose connective tissue and pericranium (SCALP).
subcutis: Another name for the hypodermis, the fatty layer under the skin.
t-cell: Lymphocytes that mature in the thymus and drive cell-mediated immunity: helper T cells coordinate, cytotoxic T cells kill infected cells.
thoracic-duct: The largest lymphatic vessel. It drains lymph from most of the body up through the thorax into the left venous angle (subclavian and internal jugular veins).
vitamin: Organic nutrients needed in small amounts, mostly as coenzymes; fat-soluble (A, D, E, K) or water-soluble (B group, C).
z-line: The dark line in the middle of each I band, where the thin filaments are anchored; the sarcomere runs from one Z line to the next.
abduct: Moves a limb or part away from the midline of the body; the opposite of adduct.
accessory-nerve: Cranial nerve XI, which supplies the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius; it crosses the posterior triangle of the neck, where it can be injured.
achille: The Achilles (ankle) reflex: tapping the Achilles tendon makes the calf contract and the foot plantar-flex, testing S1 through the tibial nerve.
anterior-compartment: A group of muscles in front of a limb segment, such as the leg's anterior compartment (dorsiflexors, deep fibular nerve) or the arm's (flexors).
backbone: In biochemistry, the repeating chain that holds a polymer together, such as the sugar–phosphate backbone of DNA or the peptide backbone of a protein.
bregma: The point on the skull where the coronal and sagittal sutures meet, the site of the anterior fontanelle.
carotid-sheath: A tube of deep cervical fascia in the neck containing the common and internal carotid arteries, the internal jugular vein and the vagus nerve.
cholesterol: A sterol lipid that stiffens cell membranes and is the precursor of steroid hormones, bile acids and vitamin D.
common-fibular-nerve: A terminal branch of the sciatic nerve that winds round the neck of the fibula, where injury causes foot drop.
cortex: The outer layer of an organ or structure, such as the hair cortex (the bulk of the hair), the lymph node cortex or the cerebral cortex.
crossbridge-cycle: The repeating cycle of contraction: myosin binds actin, the power stroke pulls the filament, ATP detaches the head, and ATP hydrolysis re-cocks it.
exocrine-gland: Glands that secrete onto a surface or into a cavity through ducts, such as sweat, sebaceous and salivary glands.
femoral-vein: The main deep vein of the thigh, continuing from the popliteal vein; it lies medial to the femoral artery in the femoral triangle.
free-nerve-ending: Unencapsulated sensory endings in the epidermis and dermis that sense pain, temperature and crude touch.
innate: Present from birth, not learned: innate reflexes such as withdrawal (as opposed to acquired ones), or the innate (non-specific) immune response.
krause: Krause end bulbs: small encapsulated nerve endings in the dermis and mucous membranes, traditionally linked to cold and, in the practicum, to pressure.
kymograph: A rotating-drum recorder that traces muscle contractions over time in the classic frog wet lab.
length-tension: The relationship between a muscle's resting length and the force it can produce: maximal at optimal overlap of actin and myosin, less when too short or stretched.
maximal-tension: The greatest force a muscle produces once every fibre has been recruited; further increases in stimulus strength add nothing.
muscle-action-potential: The electrical impulse that spreads along the sarcolemma and down the T-tubules after the end-plate potential reaches threshold, triggering calcium release.
myoepithelial-cell: Contractile, star-shaped cells around the secretory units of glands (such as sweat and mammary glands) that squeeze the secretion out.
myofiber: A muscle fibre: one whole skeletal muscle cell, as opposed to a myofibril inside it.
nebulin: A giant protein lying along the thin filament from the Z disc that acts as a ruler, setting the length of the actin filament.
patella: The kneecap, the largest sesamoid bone, in the quadriceps tendon; it improves the leverage of knee extension.
patellar: The patellar (knee-jerk) reflex: tapping the patellar ligament stretches the quadriceps, which contracts to extend the knee, testing L3–L4 via the femoral nerve.
periosteum: The fibrous membrane covering bone (except articular surfaces), carrying nerves and vessels; its inner layer makes new bone.
plasma-cell: Terminally differentiated B cells that secrete antibodies; they have an eccentric 'clock-face' nucleus and lots of rough ER.
power-stroke: The step of the crossbridge cycle in which the myosin head pivots, pulling the actin filament toward the centre of the sarcomere.
pressure-and-vibration: Deep touch sensations, sensed mainly by the large Pacinian (Vater–Pacini) corpuscles in the deep dermis and hypodermis.
pterion: The H-shaped junction of the frontal, parietal, sphenoid and temporal bones on the side of the skull; the middle meningeal artery lies beneath it, so a blow here can cause an extradural bleed.
reflex-arc: The pathway of a reflex: receptor, sensory neuron, integration centre in the CNS, motor neuron and effector.
replication: The copying of DNA before cell division: each strand serves as a template for a new one (semi-conservative replication).
sebum: The oily secretion of sebaceous glands that lubricates and waterproofs the hair and skin.
secretory-portion: The part of a gland that makes the secretion, as opposed to the duct that carries it away; in sweat glands it is the coiled deep end.
serca: The sarco/endoplasmic reticulum Ca²⁺-ATPase, the pump that uses ATP to return calcium to the SR so the muscle relaxes.
stereocilia: Very long, non-motile microvilli on the epithelium of the epididymis (absorption) and inner-ear hair cells (sensing).
sternal-angle: The angle between the manubrium and body of the sternum, where the second rib joins, at the level of the T4/T5 disc; ribs are counted from here.
subclavian-artery: The main artery to the upper limb. It arches over the first rib behind the scalenus anterior and becomes the axillary artery.
syndesmosis: A fibrous joint in which bones are joined by a ligament or interosseous membrane, such as the distal tibiofibular joint.
terminal-branche: The final branches into which a nerve or artery divides, such as the five terminal branches of the brachial plexus.
troponin-c: The calcium-binding part of troponin; when Ca²⁺ binds it, tropomyosin shifts off actin's binding sites and contraction can start.
uterus: The hollow muscular organ in which the embryo implants and grows, with a thick smooth-muscle wall (myometrium) and a lining (endometrium).
viscerocranium: The facial skeleton: the maxillae, mandible, zygomatic, nasal, lacrimal and palatine bones, the inferior nasal conchae and the vomer.
water: The main component of the body (about 60%), the solvent for nearly all biochemical reactions; its polarity and hydrogen bonds shape proteins and membranes.
wet-lab: The hands-on frog practicum in which a real gastrocnemius muscle is stimulated and its contractions recorded, unlike the PhysioEx dry lab.
active-tension: The force a muscle generates by its own contraction (crossbridges), as opposed to the passive tension of stretched elastic tissue.
all-or-none: The rule that a single muscle fibre (or an action potential) responds fully or not at all once threshold is reached; a whole muscle grades force by recruitment.
anisotropic: Polarizes light. In muscle, the dark A band (myosin) is anisotropic.
appendage: Structures attached to a main part; the skin appendages are the hairs, nails, and sweat and sebaceous glands.
autonomic-nervous-system: The involuntary part of the nervous system (sympathetic and parasympathetic) that controls smooth muscle, cardiac muscle and glands.
axilla: The armpit, a pyramid-shaped space between the arm and chest wall holding the axillary vessels, brachial plexus and lymph nodes; its skin has apocrine sweat glands.
bicep-tendon: The tendon of biceps brachii, felt in the cubital fossa; tapping it tests the biceps reflex (C5–C6).
blood-supply: The arteries that bring blood to a structure and the veins that drain it.
brachial-artery: The main artery of the arm, continuing from the axillary artery; its pulse is felt in the cubital fossa (used for blood pressure) before it divides into radial and ulnar arteries.
cross-striation: The regular alternating light and dark bands across skeletal and cardiac muscle fibres.
cubital-fossa: The triangular hollow in front of the elbow containing (lateral to medial) the biceps tendon, the brachial artery and the median nerve.
dorsum-of-the-foot: The upper surface of the foot, where the dorsalis pedis pulse is felt.
eccrine: Sweat glands that secrete watery sweat directly onto the skin surface by merocrine secretion.
elastic-fiber: Connective-tissue fibres of elastin that stretch and recoil, found in the skin, lungs, arteries and elastic cartilage.
eleidin: A clear protein in the stratum lucidum, formed from keratohyalin, which gives that layer its translucent look.
embryoblast: The inner cell mass of the blastocyst, which becomes the embryo itself.
end-plate-potential: The local depolarization of the motor end plate when acetylcholine opens its receptor channels; normally large enough to fire a muscle action potential.
epiblast: The upper layer of the bilaminar embryonic disc (tall columnar cells facing the amniotic cavity), which forms all three germ layers.
epiphysis: The expanded end of a long bone, filled with spongy bone and red marrow and capped with articular cartilage.
fibula: The slender lateral bone of the leg; it bears little weight but gives attachment to muscles and forms the lateral malleolus.
fusiform: Spindle-shaped, thick in the middle and tapering at both ends, like smooth muscle cells or a fusiform muscle.
hinge: A synovial joint that moves in one plane only (flexion and extension), like the elbow and the interphalangeal joints.
hyoid: The U-shaped bone in the neck that doesn't articulate with any other bone; it anchors the tongue and the supra- and infrahyoid muscles.
ilium: The broad upper part of the hip bone, ending in the iliac crest.
intercostal-space: The space between two adjacent ribs, holding the intercostal muscles, nerve, artery and vein.
isotropic: Not polarizing light. In muscle, the light I band (thin actin filaments) is isotropic.
lambda: The point on the back of the skull where the sagittal and lambdoid sutures meet, the site of the posterior fontanelle.
laminae: Thin plates; in a vertebra, the two laminae form the back of the vertebral arch between the pedicles and the spinous process.
median-plane: The single vertical plane through the midline that divides the body into equal right and left halves.
meissner: Meissner's corpuscles: encapsulated light-touch receptors in the dermal papillae, especially of the fingertips.
middle-meningeal-artery: A branch of the maxillary artery that enters the skull through the foramen spinosum and runs under the pterion; its tear causes an extradural haematoma.
muscle-length: The starting (resting) length of a muscle, which sets how much its filaments overlap and so how much force it can produce.
myofilament: The protein filaments inside myofibrils: thin (actin) and thick (myosin), whose sliding produces contraction.
neurocranium: The part of the skull that encloses the brain: the frontal, ethmoid, sphenoid and occipital bones and the paired temporal and parietal bones.
nodal: Nodal, a signalling protein that sets up the left–right axis of the early embryo; also refers to nodes, such as lymph nodes.
palm-and-sole: The palms and soles, covered by thick skin: a heavy stratum corneum, a stratum lucidum, many sweat glands, and no hair.
passive-tension: The force from stretching a muscle's elastic elements (mainly titin and connective tissue) when it is pulled beyond its resting length.
peptide-bond: The amide bond joining two amino acids, formed between the carboxyl group of one and the amino group of the next with the release of water.
pivot: A synovial joint allowing rotation around one axis, like the atlanto-axial joint and the proximal radio-ulnar joint.
platelet: Small anucleate fragments of megakaryocytes that plug damaged vessels and start blood clotting.
pubis: The front part of the hip bone; the two pubic bones meet at the pubic symphysis.
pupillary-light: The pupillary light reflex: light in one eye makes both pupils constrict (direct and consensual), via the optic (II) and oculomotor (III) nerves.
rotator-cuff: Four muscles (supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor, subscapularis) whose tendons hold the head of the humerus in the shoulder socket.
sartorius: The longest muscle in the body, crossing the front of the thigh from the anterior superior iliac spine to the medial tibia; it forms the lateral border of the femoral triangle.
satellite-cell: Muscle stem cells lying between the sarcolemma and basal lamina of skeletal fibres, which can divide to repair damaged muscle.
somite: Paired blocks of paraxial mesoderm along the embryo, which divide into sclerotome (vertebrae, ribs), dermatome (dermis) and myotome (muscle).
spleen: The lymphoid organ in the left upper abdomen that filters blood: red pulp removes old red cells, white pulp mounts immune responses.
submandibular: Below the mandible: the submandibular triangle, gland and lymph nodes.
surface-specialization: Features of an epithelium's free surface such as microvilli, cilia or keratinization, used with layers and cell shape to classify it.
sweat-gland: Coiled tubular glands in the skin: eccrine glands cool the body with watery sweat; apocrine glands in the axilla and groin open into hair follicles.
trophoblast: The outer cell layer of the blastocyst, which invades the uterine wall and forms the embryonic part of the placenta.
upper-motor-neuron: Neurons from the brain to the spinal cord that control lower motor neurons; damage gives spasticity, hyperreflexia and a positive Babinski sign.
vomer: A thin flat bone forming the lower and back part of the bony nasal septum.
acetabulum: The cup-shaped socket on the side of the hip bone, formed by the ilium, ischium and pubis, that holds the head of the femur.
agranulocyte: White blood cells without visible granules: lymphocytes and monocytes.
anaerobic-glycolysis: Breaking glucose down to lactic acid without oxygen; fast but yields only 2 ATP per glucose, fuelling about 30–40 seconds of intense effort.
anatomical-position: The standard reference posture: standing upright, facing forward, arms at the sides with palms forward and feet together. All directions are described from it.
ascite: Ascites: fluid collecting in the peritoneal cavity, for example when low albumin lowers the plasma oncotic pressure (as in cirrhosis or nephrotic syndrome).
basal-layer: The deepest cell layer of an epithelium, on the basement membrane; in the epidermis it is the stratum basale.
basis: The base of a cone- or pyramid-shaped structure, opposite its apex.
behind-the-medial-malleolus: The groove behind the inner ankle bone, through which (front to back) the tibialis posterior, flexor digitorum longus, posterior tibial artery and vein, tibial nerve and flexor hallucis longus pass.
calmodulin: A calcium-binding protein that, in smooth muscle, activates myosin light-chain kinase to start contraction (smooth muscle has no troponin).
canalis-nervi-hypoglossi: The hypoglossal canal, a channel in the occipital bone above each condyle that carries the hypoglossal nerve (CN XII).
carpal-tunnel: The passage at the front of the wrist, between the carpal bones and the flexor retinaculum, carrying the long finger flexor tendons and the median nerve.
cephalic-vein: A superficial vein running up the lateral side of the arm and in the deltopectoral groove to join the axillary vein.
collagen-fiber: Strong, flexible fibres of collagen protein, the main fibre of connective tissue, resisting pulling forces.
collum-costae: The neck of a rib, the short part between its head and tubercle.
dense-regular-connective-tissue: Connective tissue with collagen fibres packed in parallel, very strong in one direction; it forms tendons and ligaments.
dermal-papilla: A projection of dermis into the epidermis; in a hair follicle, the papilla at the base of the bulb that nourishes the growing hair.
dermal-root-sheath: The outer connective-tissue layer of a hair follicle, continuous with the dermis; the arrector pili attaches to it.
distract-the-subject: In reflex testing, giving the person something else to focus on (or Jendrassik's manoeuvre) so conscious tensing doesn't suppress the reflex.
dorsal-rami: The posterior branches of the spinal nerves, supplying the deep back muscles (such as erector spinae) and the skin of the back.
dorsiflexion: Bending the foot upward at the ankle, toward the shin; done by the anterior leg muscles via the deep fibular nerve.
edema: Swelling from excess fluid in the tissue spaces, for example when low plasma albumin lets fluid leak out of capillaries.
eumelanin: The brown-black melanin made by melanocytes, which protects the skin's cells from ultraviolet light.
fertilization: The fusion of sperm and egg, usually in the uterine tube, forming a diploid zygote.
foramen-jugulare: The jugular foramen, between the petrous temporal and occipital bones, carrying CN IX, X and XI and the internal jugular vein.
glycolipid: Lipids with a sugar attached, on the outer surface of cell membranes, where they help in cell recognition.
hair-shaft: The part of a hair above the skin surface: dead keratinized cells in cuticle, cortex and (in thick hairs) medulla.
hip-bone: The os coxae, formed by the fused ilium, ischium and pubis, which meet at the acetabulum.
inferior-thyroid-artery: A branch of the thyrocervical trunk supplying the thyroid gland; it is closely related to the recurrent laryngeal nerve.
inversion: Turning the sole of the foot inward, toward the midline; the opposite of eversion.
isotonic-contraction: A contraction in which the muscle changes length while its tension stays about the same, because its force is enough to move the load.
keratohyalin-granule: Dark basophilic granules in the stratum granulosum that help bundle keratin filaments as the cells die and keratinize.
lactic-acid: The product of anaerobic glycolysis, formed from pyruvate when oxygen is short; it builds up in hard-working muscle.
lamina-cribrosa: The cribriform plate of the ethmoid bone, perforated by small holes that carry the olfactory nerve fibres (CN I) into the nasal cavity.
lower-motor-neuron: The motor neuron from the spinal cord or brainstem to the muscle; damage gives weakness, wasting, low tone and absent reflexes.
maximal-tetanic-tension: The force reached when further increases in stimulus frequency no longer raise it: the strongest contraction a muscle can produce.
mediastinum: The central compartment of the thorax between the lungs, containing the heart, great vessels, trachea, oesophagus and thymus.
merkel-s-disc: Unencapsulated light-touch receptors formed by a sensory nerve ending on a Merkel cell in the basal epidermis.
metabolism: All the chemical reactions in the body: catabolism breaks molecules down for energy, anabolism builds them up.
myomesin: A protein of the M line that holds the thick filaments in register.
neural-crest: Cells from the edges of the neural folds that migrate widely to form peripheral ganglia, melanocytes, the adrenal medulla and much of the facial skeleton.
neural-tube: The tube formed when the neural plate folds and closes, which becomes the brain and spinal cord; failed closure causes defects such as spina bifida.
nourished-by-diffusion: How avascular tissues (epithelium, cartilage) get oxygen and nutrients: they diffuse in from capillaries in the nearby connective tissue.
one-or-two-central-nuclei: The nuclear pattern of cardiac muscle cells, unlike the many peripheral nuclei of skeletal muscle fibres.
onto-the-skin-surface: Where eccrine sweat glands open: their ducts reach the skin surface directly, whereas apocrine glands open into hair follicles.
patellar-ligament: The continuation of the quadriceps tendon from the patella to the tibial tuberosity; tapping it gives the knee-jerk reflex.
phosphate-group: A phosphorus atom bound to four oxygens; phosphate groups link nucleotides into DNA and RNA and carry energy in ATP.
polygonal-cell: Many-sided cells, like the keratinocytes of the stratum spinosum, shaped by pressing against their neighbours.
popliteal-vein: The deep vein behind the knee, formed from the tibial veins, which continues up as the femoral vein.
sliding-filament-theory: The model of contraction: thin actin filaments slide over thick myosin filaments toward the centre of the sarcomere, so the sarcomere shortens but the filaments don't.
stratified-squamous: Epithelium of many layers with flat surface cells, resisting abrasion: keratinized in the skin, non-keratinized in the mouth, oesophagus and vagina.
submental: Below the chin: the submental triangle (between the anterior bellies of the digastrics and the hyoid) and its lymph nodes.
superficial-vein: Veins in the subcutaneous tissue, such as the great saphenous and cephalic veins, connected to the deep veins by perforating veins.
surface-cell-shape: The shape of the top layer of cells (squamous, cuboidal or columnar), which names the type of epithelium.
syncytiotrophoblast: The outer multinucleated layer of the trophoblast that invades the uterine lining and makes hCG.
talus: The ankle bone that carries the body's weight from the tibia to the foot, articulating above with the leg bones and below with the calcaneus.
thick-capsule: A heavy connective-tissue capsule, as around the Pacinian corpuscle, whose many lamellae make it a fast-adapting pressure and vibration sensor.
thin-capsule: A delicate capsule of a few flattened cells, as around Meissner's corpuscles and Ruffini endings.
tonofibril: Bundles of keratin intermediate filaments (tonofilaments) in keratinocytes that anchor at desmosomes, giving the stratum spinosum its strength.
urinary-bladder: The hollow muscular organ storing urine, lined by transitional epithelium (urothelium) that stretches as it fills.
vater-pacini-corpuscle: The Pacinian corpuscle: a large oval receptor in the deep dermis and hypodermis with an onion-like capsule, sensing deep pressure and vibration.
wide-lumen: A broad central space, like that of apocrine sweat glands compared with the narrow lumen of eccrine glands.
wrist-drop: Inability to extend the wrist and fingers from radial nerve injury, typically in the radial groove from a mid-shaft humerus fracture.
acetylcholinesterase: The enzyme in the synaptic cleft that breaks acetylcholine down, ending its signal at the neuromuscular junction.
acromion: The flat outer end of the scapular spine, forming the point of the shoulder and articulating with the clavicle.
aerobic-respiration: The full oxidation of glucose, fatty acids and amino acids in mitochondria using oxygen, giving about 32 ATP per glucose; it powers long, steady exercise.
anchoring-fibril: Type VII collagen fibrils that fasten the basal lamina to the underlying dermis.
anterior-triangle: The front region of the neck, in front of the sternocleidomastoid, subdivided into the submandibular, submental, carotid and muscular triangles.
apical-surface: The free surface of an epithelial cell facing the lumen or outside, where microvilli, cilia and stereocilia project.
apocrine-sweat-gland: Large sweat glands with a wide lumen in the axilla, areola and anogenital region, opening into hair follicles; active after puberty.
articular-cartilage: The smooth hyaline cartilage covering the ends of bones in synovial joints, reducing friction and absorbing shock.
ball-and-socket: A synovial joint where a round head fits into a cup, allowing movement in every direction, like the shoulder and hip.
below-piriformis: The part of the greater sciatic foramen below the piriformis muscle, through which the sciatic nerve, inferior gluteal vessels and nerves, and pudendal nerve leave the pelvis.
calcaneus: The heel bone, the largest tarsal bone; the Achilles tendon inserts on its tuberosity, and its sustentaculum tali supports the talus.
catabolism: The metabolic pathways that break large molecules into smaller ones, releasing energy (such as glycolysis and fatty-acid oxidation).
center-of-the-a-band: The middle of the A band, holding the lighter H zone and, at its centre, the M line.
clonus: Rhythmic, repeated involuntary muscle contractions after a sudden stretch, a sign of an upper motor neuron lesion.
common-fibular: The common fibular (peroneal) nerve, a branch of the sciatic nerve that winds round the fibular neck and divides into the superficial and deep fibular nerves.
consensual: The consensual light reflex: shining light into one eye also constricts the pupil of the other eye.
costae-spuriae: False ribs (8–12), whose cartilages don't reach the sternum directly; ribs 11 and 12 are 'floating'.
cramp: A sudden, involuntary, sustained and painful contraction of a muscle, usually in the calf.
cuticle: A thin outer covering: the hair cuticle of overlapping flat keratinized cells, or the eponychium at the base of a nail.
deep-fibular-nerve: A branch of the common fibular nerve that supplies the anterior leg muscles (dorsiflexors) and the skin between the first two toes.
deep-vein: Veins running with the arteries beneath the deep fascia, such as the femoral and popliteal veins; the site of deep vein thrombosis.
dendrite: Branching processes of a neuron that receive signals and carry them toward the cell body.
depletion: Running out of something, as in the depletion of creatine phosphate, ATP or glycogen that contributes to muscle fatigue.
dystrophin: A protein under the sarcolemma linking the actin cytoskeleton to the extracellular matrix, transmitting force and protecting the membrane; its absence causes Duchenne muscular dystrophy.
epidermal-ridge: Downward folds of the epidermis between the dermal papillae, forming the ridges of fingerprints in thick skin.
epididymis: The coiled duct behind the testis where sperm mature and are stored, lined by pseudostratified epithelium with stereocilia.
eponychium: The cuticle: the fold of stratum corneum extending from the proximal nail fold onto the nail plate.
femoral-triangle: The region of the upper front thigh bounded by the inguinal ligament, sartorius and adductor longus, containing (lateral to medial) the femoral nerve, artery and vein and the femoral canal.
flat-bone: Thin, flattened bones such as the skull vault, sternum and scapula: two plates of compact bone with spongy bone (diploë) between.
foot-drop: Inability to dorsiflex the foot, usually from injury to the common fibular nerve at the neck of the fibula; the toes drag and the patient lifts the knee high to walk.
foramen-magnum: The large opening in the occipital bone where the medulla oblongata joins the spinal cord, with the vertebral arteries and the spinal roots of CN XI.
foramen-ovale: An opening in the greater wing of the sphenoid that carries the mandibular nerve (V3); also, in the fetal heart, the opening between the atria.
foramen-stylomastoideum: The stylomastoid foramen, between the styloid and mastoid processes, where the facial nerve (CN VII) leaves the skull.
gastrulation: The third-week process in which epiblast cells migrate through the primitive streak to form the three germ layers.
glabella: The smooth area of the frontal bone between the eyebrows, above the nose.
great-saphenous-vein: The longest vein in the body, a superficial vein running up the medial leg and thigh from in front of the medial malleolus to the femoral vein.
greater-sciatic-foramen: The opening from the pelvis to the gluteal region, divided by the piriformis: the superior gluteal vessels and nerve leave above it; the sciatic nerve and others below.
hypoblast: The lower layer of the bilaminar embryonic disc (small cuboidal cells facing the blastocoele), which contributes to the yolk sac.
hypoglossal-nerve: Cranial nerve XII, which leaves the skull through the hypoglossal canal and supplies the muscles of the tongue.
hyponychium: The thickened epidermis under the free distal edge of the nail.
immune-cell: Cells that defend the body; in the skin, Langerhans cells capture antigens and carry them to lymph nodes.
infraorbital: Below the orbit: the infraorbital foramen, nerve (from V2) and artery, which supply the cheek and upper lip.
inner-cell-mass: The cluster of cells inside the blastocyst (the embryoblast) that becomes the embryo.
into-a-hair-follicle: Where apocrine sweat glands and sebaceous glands open, rather than directly onto the skin.
irregular-dark-transverse-line: How intercalated discs look in cardiac muscle: dark, step-like lines crossing the fibres where two cells join.
kidney-shaped: Bean-shaped: like the large vertebral bodies of the lumbar spine or the nucleus of a monocyte.
lacunar-ligament: A crescent-shaped ligament from the inguinal ligament to the pectineal line, forming the medial border of the femoral ring.
lateral-surface: The side surface of an epithelial cell, facing its neighbours, where the junctional complex (tight junctions, adherens junctions, desmosomes) sits.
lefty1: A signalling protein in the early embryo that restricts Nodal to the left side, helping to set up left–right asymmetry.
long-bone: Bones longer than they are wide, such as the femur and humerus: a shaft (diaphysis) of compact bone and two ends (epiphyses).
m-iliopsoas: Iliopsoas, the iliacus and psoas major together: the strongest flexor of the hip, inserting on the lesser trochanter.
medial-border: The inner edge of a structure; for the anatomical snuffbox, the tendon of extensor pollicis longus.
medial-circumflex-femoral-artery: A branch of the deep femoral artery that winds round the femoral neck and is the main blood supply to the femoral head; femoral neck fractures can tear it.
merkel-corpuscle: A Merkel cell together with its disc-shaped sensory nerve ending in the basal epidermis, a slowly adapting light-touch receptor.
mitosis: Cell division that gives two genetically identical daughter cells; in the epidermis it happens mainly in the stratum basale.
more-actin-and-myosin: More overlap of actin and myosin, or more contractile protein, lets more crossbridges form and so more force.
myoglobin: An oxygen-storing protein in muscle fibres, related to haemoglobin, that gives red (slow, oxidative) muscle its colour.
myotome: The part of a somite that forms skeletal muscle; also the group of muscles supplied by one spinal nerve root.
non-striated: Without cross-striations, because the actin and myosin are not arranged in sarcomeres: smooth muscle.
nucleosome: The basic unit of chromatin: about 147 base pairs of DNA wrapped around an octamer of histone proteins.
oncotic-pressure: The osmotic pressure made by plasma proteins (mainly albumin) that holds fluid inside the capillaries; when it falls, fluid leaks out as oedema.
osteocyte: Mature bone cells sitting in lacunae in the bone matrix, connected through canaliculi, which maintain the bone and sense strain.
pacinian-corpuscle: Large, onion-like encapsulated receptors in the deep dermis and hypodermis that sense deep pressure and vibration.
papillary-dermis: The thin upper layer of the dermis: loose connective tissue forming the dermal papillae, with capillaries and Meissner's corpuscles.
parotid-gland: The largest salivary gland, in front of and below the ear; the facial nerve branches pass through it. It is supplied by CN IX.
peripheral-protein: Membrane proteins loosely attached to the inner or outer surface of the lipid bilayer, not embedded in it.
phospholipid: Lipids with a polar phosphate head and two fatty-acid tails, which arrange themselves into the bilayer of cell membranes.
pitx2: A transcription factor switched on by Nodal on the left side of the embryo, which directs left-sided development of organs such as the heart and gut.
platysma: A thin, broad muscle of facial expression in the superficial neck that tenses the skin of the neck; supplied by the facial nerve.
pleural-effusion: Fluid collecting in the pleural space around the lung, for example when low albumin reduces plasma oncotic pressure.
posterior-compartment: The group of muscles at the back of a limb segment, such as the leg's calf muscles (plantar flexors, tibial nerve) or the arm's extensors.
posture: The position the body holds; skeletal muscles keep it with sustained, low-level contraction (tone) against gravity.
primitive-streak: A groove on the epiblast in week 3 through which cells migrate in gastrulation to form mesoderm and endoderm.
purely-ketogenic: Amino acids (leucine and lysine) that can only be broken down to acetyl-CoA or ketone bodies, never to glucose.
radial-artery: The forearm artery on the thumb side, whose pulse is felt at the wrist; it forms the deep palmar arch.
relaxation-phase: The last phase of a twitch, when calcium is pumped back into the SR and the muscle's tension falls.
rhomboid: Diamond-shaped, like the anterior fontanelle; also the rhomboid muscles, which pull the scapula toward the spine.
ribosome: The cell's protein factory, made of rRNA and protein, which reads mRNA and links amino acids into a chain.
right-lymphatic-duct: A short lymph vessel draining the right side of the head, neck, thorax and right arm into the right venous angle.
rigor-mortis: The stiffening of muscles after death: without ATP, myosin heads stay locked to actin.
ringer-lactate: A balanced salt solution used to keep the frog muscle and nerve alive and moist during the wet lab.
saddle: A synovial joint whose two saddle-shaped surfaces allow movement in two planes, such as the carpometacarpal joint of the thumb.
saphenous-nerve: The longest branch of the femoral nerve, a sensory nerve running with the great saphenous vein to the skin of the medial leg and foot.
sigmoid: S-shaped, as in the sigmoid sinus of the skull (which becomes the internal jugular vein) or the sigmoid colon.
simple-branched-acinar: A gland whose rounded secretory sacs (acini) branch from one unbranched duct, like the sebaceous glands.
simple-coiled-tubular: A gland formed by a single long tube whose secretory end is coiled into a ball, like the sweat glands.
spina-bifida: A neural tube defect in which the vertebral arches of the lower vertebrae fail to fuse; low maternal folic acid is the major preventable cause.
stratum-granulosum: The epidermal layer above the spinosum: flattened keratinocytes with keratohyalin granules and lamellar granules that make the skin's waterproof barrier.
stratum-malpighii: The stratum basale and stratum spinosum together, the living, dividing layers of the epidermis.
stratum-papillare: The papillary layer of the dermis: thin, loose connective tissue in the dermal papillae, with capillary loops and Meissner's corpuscles.
stretch-reflex: A monosynaptic reflex: stretching a muscle excites its muscle spindles, whose Ia afferents fire motor neurons to the same muscle so it contracts, as in the knee jerk.
supraorbital: Above the orbit: the supraorbital margin, foramen (or notch), nerve and vessels, supplying the forehead.
sutura-lambdoidea: The lambdoid suture, between the occipital bone and the two parietal bones at the back of the skull.
sweat-pore: The opening of an eccrine sweat gland duct on the skin surface.
tight-junction: A belt-like seal between the tops of neighbouring epithelial cells that blocks the space between them, controlling what passes.
triad: In skeletal muscle, one T-tubule flanked by two terminal cisternae of the sarcoplasmic reticulum, where the action potential triggers calcium release.
tuberculum-costae: The tubercle of a rib, a knob on its back that articulates with the transverse process of its own vertebra.
type-i-collagen: The most abundant collagen, forming strong fibres in bone, tendons, ligaments, the dermis and organ capsules.
unencapsulated: Nerve endings without a connective-tissue capsule, such as free nerve endings and Merkel discs.
unfused-tetanus: Incomplete tetanus: stimuli come fast enough that twitches summate, but the muscle partly relaxes between them, giving a wavy plateau.
v-jugularis-interna: The internal jugular vein (vena jugularis interna), the main vein draining the brain, leaving the skull through the jugular foramen.
vastus-medialis: One of the four quadriceps muscles, on the inner front of the thigh, which extends the knee and steadies the patella.
visceral-muscle: Smooth muscle in the walls of hollow organs, such as the gut, bladder and uterus.
adductor-longus: A medial thigh muscle that adducts the hip, running from the body of the pubis to the linea aspera; it forms the medial border of the femoral triangle.
adipocyte: Fat cells, each mostly one large lipid droplet with the nucleus pushed to the edge; they store energy and insulate.
amniotic-cavity: The fluid-filled sac above the epiblast that surrounds and cushions the embryo.
anastomosis: A connection between two vessels (or nerves) that gives an alternative route for blood.
angulus-costae: The angle of a rib, where its shaft turns sharply forward; the most common site of rib fracture.
ansa-cervicalis: A loop of nerve fibres from C1–C3 that supplies the infrahyoid (strap) muscles of the neck.
antagonist: A muscle that opposes the movement of another (the agonist), such as the triceps against the biceps; in reflexes it is inhibited reciprocally.
anterior-talofibular-ligament: A lateral ankle ligament from the fibula to the talus, the ligament most often torn in an inversion sprain.
anulus-fibrosus: The tough outer ring of an intervertebral disc: concentric lamellae of fibrocartilage, their fibres crossing obliquely, around the nucleus pulposus.
asterion: The point on the side of the skull where the parietal, occipital and temporal (mastoid) bones meet.
basilic: The basilic vein, a superficial vein on the medial side of the arm that joins the brachial veins to form the axillary vein.
bell-s-palsy: Sudden weakness or paralysis of one side of the face from facial nerve (CN VII) dysfunction, often near the stylomastoid foramen.
canalis-caroticus: The carotid canal in the petrous temporal bone, through which the internal carotid artery enters the skull.
caput-costae: The head of a rib, which articulates with the bodies of its own vertebra and the one above.
cavernous-sinus: A venous sinus beside the sella turcica containing the internal carotid artery and CN III, IV, V1, V2 and VI; facial infections can spread to it.
claw-hand: A hand posture from ulnar nerve injury: the ring and little fingers hyperextend at the knuckles and flex at the finger joints because their lumbricals and interossei are paralysed.
cleavage: The rapid mitotic divisions of the zygote into smaller cells (blastomeres) without growth, leading to the morula.
compartment-syndrome: Rising pressure inside a closed fascial compartment that squeezes its vessels and nerves, threatening the muscles; treated urgently by fasciotomy.
complete-tetanus: Fused tetanus: stimulation so fast that there is no relaxation between stimuli, giving a smooth maximal contraction.
contractile-filament: The actin and myosin filaments that slide past each other to make a muscle cell contract.
contralateral: On the opposite side of the body from a reference point.
corpus-vertebrae: The vertebral body, the weight-bearing cylinder at the front of a vertebra, joined to its neighbours by the intervertebral discs.
cytotrophoblast: The inner, cellular layer of the trophoblast, whose cells divide and join the syncytiotrophoblast.
dense-granule: Dark, densely staining secretory granules in a cell, such as those of Merkel cells that release signals to their nerve ending.
dermatome: The part of a somite that forms the dermis; also the area of skin supplied by one spinal nerve root.
desquamation: The shedding of dead cells from the surface of the stratum corneum.
direct-phosphorylation: Making ATP directly from creatine phosphate and ADP (via creatine kinase), the fastest energy source, lasting about 10–15 seconds.
distal-end: The end of a bone or structure farther from the trunk or from its origin.
dorsal-root: The posterior root of a spinal nerve, carrying sensory fibres into the spinal cord, with their cell bodies in the dorsal root ganglion.
down-the-t-tubule: How the action potential travels in excitation–contraction coupling: along the sarcolemma and down the T-tubules into the fibre.
endocrine-gland: Ductless glands that release hormones directly into the blood, such as the thyroid, pituitary and adrenal glands.
extend-the-hip: Moving the thigh backward at the hip, done mainly by the gluteus maximus and the hamstrings.
fasciotomy: Surgically cutting open the fascia of a compartment to relieve the pressure of compartment syndrome.
femoral-artery-and-vein: The main vessels of the thigh, lying in the femoral triangle with the artery lateral to the vein; the femoral pulse is felt just below the inguinal ligament.
fine-reticular-fiber: Thin branching fibres of type III collagen that form delicate supporting networks, as in the endomysium and lymphoid organs.
foramen-lacerum: A jagged opening at the apex of the petrous temporal bone, closed by cartilage in life; the internal carotid artery passes across its upper surface.
foramen-rotundum: A round opening in the greater wing of the sphenoid that carries the maxillary nerve (V2).
foramen-spinosum: A small opening in the greater wing of the sphenoid, behind the foramen ovale, that carries the middle meningeal artery.
foregut: The front part of the embryonic gut, forming the pharynx, oesophagus, stomach, upper duodenum, liver, gallbladder, pancreas and respiratory tract; supplied by the coeliac trunk.
gamma-globulin: The plasma protein fraction containing the antibodies (immunoglobulins) made by plasma cells.
glassy-membrane: The thickened basement membrane between the epithelial and dermal root sheaths of a hair follicle.
golgi-tendon-organ: Receptors in tendons that sense muscle tension and inhibit the muscle when tension is very high, protecting it.
hand-of-benediction: From median nerve injury at or above the elbow: on trying to make a fist, the index and middle fingers stay straight while the ring and little fingers flex.
hard-palate: The bony front part of the roof of the mouth, formed by the maxillae and palatine bones, separating the mouth from the nasal cavity.
hiatus-sacralis: The sacral hiatus, the opening at the lower end of the sacral canal, used for caudal epidural injections.
hindgut: The last part of the embryonic gut, forming the distal third of the transverse colon down to the upper anal canal; supplied by the inferior mesenteric artery.
holocrine-secretion: Secretion in which the whole cell fills with lipid, dies and disintegrates to become the product (sebum); basal cells replace it.
hyperreflexia: Overactive reflexes from loss of descending inhibition in an upper motor neuron lesion, as after a stroke or spinal cord compression.
iliac-crest: The long curved upper border of the ilium, felt at the waist; a line between the two crests crosses L4.
infraglenoid-tubercle: A roughened area just below the shoulder socket of the scapula where the long head of triceps arises.
initiate-abduction: Starting the first 15° or so of moving the arm away from the body, the job of the supraspinatus before the deltoid takes over.
inspiration: Breathing in: the diaphragm and external intercostals enlarge the thorax so air flows into the lungs.
integral-protein: Membrane proteins embedded in, and often spanning, the lipid bilayer, such as channels, carriers and receptors.
interneuron: Neurons within the CNS that connect sensory and motor neurons; they make polysynaptic reflexes possible.
intron: Non-coding sequences in a gene, copied into pre-mRNA but cut out by splicing before translation.
ischial-tuberosity: The rough bony lump at the bottom of the ischium that you sit on; the hamstrings arise from it.
ischium: The lower back part of the hip bone, ending in the ischial tuberosity.
isometric-contraction: A contraction in which the muscle develops tension without changing length, because the load is too heavy to move or a position is being held.
jendrassik-maneuver: Hooking the fingers together and pulling just before a leg reflex is tested, to reinforce a weak reflex.
lachman: The Lachman test: with the knee bent about 20–30°, pulling the tibia forward checks the anterior cruciate ligament.
lateral-epicondyle: The bony prominence on the outer side of the lower humerus, from which the forearm extensors arise (inflamed in tennis elbow).
lateral-wall: The side wall of a cavity, such as the lateral wall of the nasal cavity or the orbit.
lefty2: A signalling protein in the left lateral-plate mesoderm of the embryo that limits Nodal signalling, helping to set left–right asymmetry.
lesser-tubercle: A small bony prominence on the front of the upper humerus where the subscapularis inserts.
long-thoracic-nerve: A nerve from C5–C7 that runs down the side of the chest wall to the serratus anterior; injury gives a winged scapula.
lower-border-of-the-mandible: The lower edge of the jaw, the upper boundary of the anterior triangle of the neck.
m-sartorius: The sartorius, the long strap muscle crossing the front of the thigh that flexes, abducts and laterally rotates the hip and flexes the knee.
mandibular-nerve: V3, the third division of the trigeminal nerve, leaving through the foramen ovale to supply the muscles of mastication and sensation to the lower face and jaw.
margo-supraorbitalis: The supraorbital margin, the upper rim of the orbit, with the supraorbital foramen or notch for the supraorbital nerve and vessels.
mechanoreceptor: A sensory receptor that responds to mechanical force such as touch, pressure, vibration or stretch.
medulla-cortex-cuticle: The three layers of a hair from the inside out: medulla (core), cortex (bulk and pigment) and cuticle (overlapping surface cells).
menisci: C-shaped pads of fibrocartilage in the knee that deepen the tibial surface and absorb shock.
metaphysis: The flared region between the epiphysis and the shaft of a long bone; in a growing bone it contains the growth plate.
midgut: The middle part of the embryonic gut, forming the second half of the duodenum to the proximal two-thirds of the transverse colon; supplied by the superior mesenteric artery.
mineral: Inorganic elements the body needs, such as calcium, phosphorus, iron, sodium and potassium, for bones, nerves, enzymes and fluid balance.
morula: A solid ball of 12–16 cells formed by cleavage about 3 days after fertilization, before it becomes a blastocyst.
muscle-twitch: A single brief contraction of a muscle in response to one stimulus: latent period, contraction, then relaxation.
navel: NAVEL, a mnemonic for the order of structures in the femoral triangle from lateral to medial: Nerve, Artery, Vein, Empty space, Lymphatics.
nephrotic-syndrome: Kidney disease with heavy protein loss in the urine; the resulting low albumin causes oedema, ascites and high blood lipids.
neural-plate: The thickened strip of ectoderm along the embryo's back, induced by the notochord, that folds to form the neural tube.
neurovascular-bundle: A nerve, artery and vein running together in a shared sheath, as in each intercostal space or the carotid sheath.
nitrogenous-base: The part of a nucleotide that carries the genetic code: purines (adenine, guanine) and pyrimidines (cytosine, thymine, uracil).
phosphodiester-bond: The bond linking the sugar of one nucleotide to the phosphate of the next, forming the sugar–phosphate backbone of DNA and RNA.
pilosebaceous-unit: A hair follicle together with its sebaceous gland and arrector pili muscle.
plantar-flex: To point the foot downward at the ankle, done mainly by the calf muscles.
poikilothermic: Cold-blooded: an animal, such as the frog used in the wet lab, whose body temperature follows its surroundings.
polyspermy: Fertilization of an egg by more than one sperm, normally prevented by the zona reaction.
popliteal-fossa: The diamond-shaped hollow behind the knee containing the popliteal artery and vein and the tibial and common fibular nerves.
posterior-intercostal-artery: Arteries running in the intercostal spaces from the back, mostly branches of the thoracic aorta, along the lower border of each rib.
pre-mrna: The first RNA copy of a gene, still containing introns, before splicing and processing into mature mRNA.
pseudostratified-ciliated-columnar: Respiratory epithelium: it looks layered but every cell touches the basement membrane; ciliated cells and goblet cells line the airways.
rectus-femoris: The only quadriceps muscle crossing both hip and knee: it flexes the hip and extends the knee.
recurrent-laryngeal-nerve: A branch of the vagus nerve that loops back up beside the trachea to supply most laryngeal muscles; damage in thyroid surgery causes hoarseness.
reflex-hammer: The small rubber hammer used to tap a tendon and elicit a stretch reflex.
rigor-state: The state in which myosin heads stay locked to actin because there is no ATP to release them; it causes rigor mortis.
rt-pcr: Reverse-transcription PCR: RNA is copied into DNA and then amplified, used to detect RNA viruses such as SARS-CoV-2.
sagittal-plane: Any vertical plane parallel to the median plane, dividing the body into unequal right and left parts.
same-side: Ipsilateral: on the same side of the body as the reference point.
sarcosome: The mitochondria of a muscle fibre, abundant between the myofibrils, especially in cardiac muscle.
sclerotome: The part of a somite that forms the vertebrae and ribs.
section-plane: The direction a tissue is cut for the microscope: longitudinal sections show long strips, transverse sections show round profiles.
sesamoid-bone: Bones that develop inside a tendon, such as the patella, which protect the tendon and improve its leverage.
single-stimulus: One electrical shock to the muscle, which produces a single twitch in the lab.
skin-surface: The outer surface of the epidermis, the stratum corneum, where sweat pores open.
spheroidea: Articulatio spheroidea, the ball-and-socket joint, which moves in every direction including rotation, like the hip and shoulder.
