spike-protein: The protein on the surface of coronaviruses that binds the ACE2 receptor and, after cleavage by host enzymes such as TMPRSS2, lets the virus enter the cell.
spinal-reflexe: Reflexes integrated in the spinal cord, which can work even when it is cut off from the brain.
spinalis: The most medial column of the erector spinae, running between the spinous processes; it extends the spine.
splicing: Cutting the introns out of pre-mRNA and joining the exons together to make mature mRNA.
stored-atp: The small amount of ATP already in a muscle fibre, enough for only about 4–6 seconds of maximal effort.
sulcus-costae: The costal groove along the lower inner border of a rib, sheltering the intercostal vein, artery and nerve.
synovial-joint: Freely movable joints with a fluid-filled cavity, articular cartilage and a capsule lined by synovial membrane, like the knee, hip and shoulder.
thenar: The thenar eminence, the muscular pad at the base of the thumb (abductor pollicis brevis, flexor pollicis brevis, opponens pollicis), supplied by the median nerve.
thumb-side: The lateral (radial) side of the forearm and hand in the anatomical position.
tmprss2: A host-cell protease on the cell surface that cleaves the coronavirus spike protein so the virus can fuse with and enter the cell.
trendelenburg-sign: When standing on the affected leg, the pelvis drops on the opposite side, showing weak hip abductors (gluteus medius and minimus, superior gluteal nerve).
type-vii-collagen: The collagen of the anchoring fibrils that fasten the basal lamina of the epidermis to the dermis.
upper-outer-quadrant: The upper outer quarter of the buttock, the safe site for intramuscular injections because it avoids the sciatic nerve.
wave-summation: Summation: a second stimulus arriving before the muscle relaxes adds a new contraction on top of the first, so tension rises.
above-piriformis: The part of the greater sciatic foramen above the piriformis muscle, through which the superior gluteal artery, vein and nerve leave the pelvis.
acrosome-reaction: The release of enzymes from the cap of the sperm head that let it penetrate the zona pellucida of the egg.
active-force: The force a muscle produces by its own crossbridges, as opposed to passive force from stretched elastic tissue.
adductor-hiatus: The gap in the adductor magnus tendon through which the femoral vessels pass to the back of the knee, becoming the popliteal vessels.
anabolism: The metabolic pathways that build complex molecules from simpler ones, using energy (such as protein and glycogen synthesis).
angulus-mandibulae: The angle of the mandible, where its body meets the ramus.
anterior-drawer: The anterior drawer test: pulling the tibia forward with the knee bent at 90° checks the anterior cruciate ligament.
anticodon: The three-base sequence on a tRNA that pairs with the matching codon on mRNA, bringing the right amino acid.
apex-ossis-sacri: The apex of the sacrum, its narrow lower end, which joins the coccyx.
arcus-alveolaris: The alveolar arch, the curved border of the maxilla or mandible holding the tooth sockets.
arcus-superciliaris: The superciliary arch, the bony ridge of the frontal bone above each orbit, under the eyebrows.
basal-surface: The surface of an epithelial cell that faces the basement membrane, anchored to it by hemidesmosomes.
bifid: Split into two, as in the bifid spinous processes of most cervical vertebrae.
bind-actin: The first step of the crossbridge cycle: once tropomyosin moves aside, the myosin head binds an active site on actin.
biocatalyst: A biological catalyst, an enzyme, which speeds up a reaction without being used up.
bulging: Bulging fontanelle: a sign of raised intracranial pressure in an infant (a sunken one suggests dehydration).
calcitonin: A hormone from the C (parafollicular) cells of the thyroid that lowers blood calcium; its action opposes parathyroid hormone.
calcium-induced-calcium-release: The cardiac mechanism of excitation–contraction coupling: calcium entering the cell triggers release of more calcium from the SR.
calsequestrin: A protein inside the sarcoplasmic reticulum that binds and stores calcium.
canalis-condylaris: The condylar canal, behind each occipital condyle, carrying an emissary vein.
capacitation: Changes to sperm in the female tract that let them undergo the acrosome reaction and fertilize the egg.
cartilaginous-joint: Joints in which bones are joined by cartilage, allowing slight movement: synchondroses (hyaline) and symphyses (fibrocartilage).
cartilago-costalis: The costal cartilage, the bar of hyaline cartilage joining a rib to the sternum or to the cartilage above.
caudal-neuropore: The lower open end of the neural tube, which closes at about day 28; failure to close causes spina bifida.
cell-junction: Structures joining cells: tight junctions seal, desmosomes and adherens junctions anchor, gap junctions connect cytoplasm.
central-nervous-system: The brain and spinal cord, which integrate information and control the body.
cervical-plexus: The network of nerves from the ventral rami of C1–C4 that supplies the skin and some muscles of the neck and, through the phrenic nerve, the diaphragm.
change-length: What a muscle does in an isotonic contraction: it shortens (concentric) or lengthens (eccentric) while moving a load.
chopart-s-joint: The transverse tarsal joint: the talonavicular and calcaneocuboid joints together, where the foot inverts and everts.
cirrhosis: Scarring of the liver that reduces its synthetic capacity, so less albumin is made and fluid collects (ascites).
clinical-relevance: How an anatomical fact matters in practice, such as which injury a structure explains or where to examine it.
cock-the-head: The step of the crossbridge cycle where ATP hydrolysis re-cocks the detached myosin head into its high-energy position, ready to bind actin again.
compaction: Packing of the very long DNA molecule into chromatin and chromosomes, starting with nucleosomes, so it fits inside the nucleus.
connexin: The transmembrane protein subunits, six of which form a connexon of a gap junction.
connexon: A channel of six connexins in the membrane; two connexons from neighbouring cells meet to form a gap-junction channel.
contraction-phase: The phase of a twitch after the latent period, when crossbridges cycle and the muscle's tension rises to its peak.
costae: Ribs: twelve pairs of curved flat bones forming the thoracic cage, each joined at the back to the vertebrae.
costae-fluctuante: Floating ribs (11 and 12), whose front ends don't attach to the sternum or another cartilage.
costae-verae: True ribs (1–7), whose costal cartilages attach directly to the sternum.
cranial-fossae: The three steps of the floor of the skull: anterior (frontal lobes), middle (temporal lobes, pituitary) and posterior (cerebellum, brainstem).
danger-triangle-of-the-face: The area around the nose and upper lip whose valveless veins connect with the cavernous sinus, so infection here can spread inside the skull.
deep-cervical-node: Lymph nodes along the internal jugular vein that receive lymph from the whole head and neck.
deep-layer: The layer of structures lying deeper beneath the surface, such as the deep layer of the back muscles or of the neck fascia.
deformity: An abnormal shape or posture of a body part, such as the hand deformities from radial, ulnar or median nerve injuries.
dense-irregular-ct: Dense irregular connective tissue: thick collagen bundles running in many directions, as in the dermis and the epimysium.
deoxyribose: The five-carbon sugar of DNA, which lacks the oxygen at carbon 2 that ribose has.
detachment: The step of the crossbridge cycle where ATP binds the myosin head and releases it from actin; without ATP the heads stay locked (rigor).
diaphysis: The shaft of a long bone: a tube of compact bone around the marrow (medullary) cavity.
down-syndrome: Trisomy 21: an extra copy of chromosome 21 (47 chromosomes), causing intellectual disability and characteristic features.
edinger-westphal-nuclei: The parasympathetic nucleus of the oculomotor nerve in the midbrain, which constricts the pupil in the light reflex.
epidermal-root-sheath: The inner, epithelial layer of a hair follicle, continuous with the epidermis, with outer and inner root sheaths.
epidural-haematoma: Bleeding between the skull and the dura, typically from a torn middle meningeal artery after a blow at the pterion.
evert: To turn the sole of the foot outward, away from the midline.
extend-the-knee: Straightening the knee, done by the quadriceps femoris (femoral nerve).
external-carotid-artery: The branch of the common carotid that supplies the face, scalp and neck through branches such as the facial, maxillary and superficial temporal arteries.
femoral-canal: The most medial compartment of the femoral sheath, holding lymphatics and fat; it is where femoral hernias pass.
fibrinogen: A plasma protein made in the liver that is converted to fibrin, the mesh of a blood clot.
first-pharyngeal-arch: The mandibular arch of the embryo, which forms the jaw, the muscles of mastication and the mandibular nerve's territory.
five-carbon-sugar: The pentose sugar of a nucleotide: deoxyribose in DNA, ribose in RNA.
folic-acid: Vitamin B9, needed for DNA synthesis; low maternal intake is the major preventable cause of neural tube defects such as spina bifida.
foramen-mentale: The mental foramen, on the outer surface of the mandible below the premolars, where the mental nerve emerges to supply the chin and lower lip.
forced-expiration: Breathing out with effort, using the internal intercostals and abdominal muscles; quiet expiration is passive.
found-only-in-thick-skin: Describes the stratum lucidum, a layer present only in the thick skin of the palms and soles.
fusiform-cell: Spindle-shaped cells, wide in the middle and tapered at both ends, such as smooth muscle cells and fibroblasts.
hair-root: The part of a hair below the skin surface, inside the follicle, ending in the hair bulb.
high-mitotic-activity: Frequent cell division, as in the stratum basale, which contains the stem cells that renew the whole epidermis.
histone: Basic proteins around which DNA is wound to form nucleosomes, packing it into chromatin.
human-genome: The complete human DNA: about 3 billion base pairs carrying roughly 20,000 protein-coding genes.
hypoalbuminemia-cause: Causes of low blood albumin: nephrotic syndrome (lost in urine), cirrhosis (less made), kwashiorkor (too little protein eaten) and pre-eclampsia.
iliocostalis: The most lateral column of the erector spinae, running from the iliac crest to the ribs; it extends the spine.
incisura-clavicularis: The clavicular notch on each side of the manubrium, where the clavicle articulates (sternoclavicular joint).
incisura-costalis-ii: The notch for the second costal cartilage, half on the manubrium and half on the body of the sternum, at the sternal angle.
incomplete-tetanus: Unfused tetanus: twitches summate but the muscle partly relaxes between stimuli, giving a wavy tension trace.
infrahyoid: Below the hyoid bone: the infrahyoid (strap) muscles that depress the hyoid and larynx, supplied by the ansa cervicalis.
inion: The external occipital protuberance, the bump at the back of the skull in the midline.
innervation: The nerve supply of a structure, which nerve it gets its motor or sensory fibres from.
ipsilateral: On the same side of the body as a reference point.
kupffer-cell: Macrophages living in the liver sinusoids that remove old red cells, bacteria and debris from the blood.
kwashiorkor: Malnutrition from severe protein deficiency, with low albumin causing oedema and a swollen belly.
l4-l5-and-l5-s1: The two lowest lumbar disc levels, where most lumbar disc herniations happen.
lacuna-musculorum: The lateral compartment under the inguinal ligament, carrying the iliopsoas muscle and the femoral nerve into the thigh.
lamellar-granule: Lipid-filled granules in the stratum granulosum that release their contents between cells, forming the skin's waterproof barrier.
lamina-externa: The outer layer of chest-wall muscles: the external intercostals and the levatores costarum, which raise the ribs in inspiration.
lamina-interna: The inner layer of chest-wall muscles: the innermost intercostals, subcostales and transversus thoracis.
lateral-border: The outer edge of a structure; for the anatomical snuffbox, the tendons of extensor pollicis brevis and abductor pollicis longus.
laterale: Lateral: on the side, farther from the midline (Latin form, as in names like ligamentum laterale).
left-supraclavicular-node: Virchow's node, a lymph node above the left clavicle where the thoracic duct ends; its enlargement can signal abdominal cancer.
ligamenta-flava: Yellow, elastic ligaments joining the laminae of adjacent vertebrae, which help straighten the spine after flexion.
lighter: Paler in staining, like the light I band and H zone of muscle compared with the dark A band.
linea-aspera: A rough ridge down the back of the femur where the adductors and hamstrings attach.
longissimus: The middle and longest column of the erector spinae, which extends and laterally bends the spine.
m-adductor-longus: Adductor longus, running from the body of the pubis to the middle third of the linea aspera; it adducts the thigh and is supplied by the obturator nerve.
m-bicep-brachii: Biceps brachii: long head from the supraglenoid tubercle, short head from the coracoid process, inserting on the radial tuberosity; it flexes the elbow and is the strongest supinator.
meatus-acusticus-internus: The internal acoustic meatus in the petrous temporal bone, carrying the facial (VII) and vestibulocochlear (VIII) nerves and the labyrinthine artery.
merkel: Merkel discs: light-touch receptors formed by a nerve ending on a Merkel cell in the basal epidermis.
merocrine-secretion: Secretion by exocytosis, the cell staying intact, as in eccrine sweat glands.
mitochondrial-dna: The small circular genome inside mitochondria (about 16.5 kb), inherited from the mother.
mucin: Large glycoproteins secreted by goblet cells and mucous glands that absorb water to form mucus.
muscle-spindle: Stretch receptors lying among the muscle fibres that sense changes in muscle length and start the stretch reflex.
n-glycosidic-bond: The bond joining a nitrogenous base to the sugar in a nucleotide.
n-ischiadicus: The sciatic nerve (nervus ischiadicus), the nerve of the frog's leg stimulated in the wet lab, and the largest nerve in the human body.
neck-of-the-fibula: The narrow part just below the head of the fibula, where the common fibular nerve winds round and is easily injured.
nissl-body: Clumps of rough endoplasmic reticulum in a neuron's cell body and dendrites, staining dark with basic dyes, where proteins are made.
one-central-nucleus: The single central nucleus of a smooth muscle cell, unlike the many peripheral nuclei of a skeletal muscle fibre.
open-into-the-hair-follicle: Where sebaceous and apocrine sweat glands release their secretions, into a hair follicle rather than onto the skin.
open-the-jaw: Depressing the mandible, done mainly by the lateral pterygoid with the suprahyoid muscles.
os-nasale: The nasal bone, one of a pair of small bones forming the bridge of the nose.
os-zygomaticum: The zygomatic (cheek) bone, forming the prominence of the cheek and part of the orbit.
osteoclast: Large multinucleated cells that resorb bone, derived from monocytes; they work with osteoblasts in remodelling.
